subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]
passage: Dear Diary, Pallavi didi came for the holidays and she is fourteen, so she makes the rules for our games. Today she said Rumi can't play hide-and-seek with us because Rumi is 'too small and cries'. Didi said, 'Go tell Rumi to go home. You're the host.' My tummy went twisty. Rumi is only one year younger than me and she hides really well. But didi is older and knows about games, so she must be right. I went and said it. Rumi didn't cry. She just walked back and sat on her steps with her chin on her knees. I kept looking at her while I counted. It was didi's rule, not mine. But I was the one who said it. — Himani

qa.q: Why did Pallavi didi say Rumi couldn't play?
qa.a: Didi said Rumi was 'too small and cries'.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when told to send Rumi home, and why go along anyway?
qa.a: Himani's tummy went twisty with unease, but Himani decided didi must be right because didi is older and knows about games.

qa.q: What choice could Himani make the next time didi gives an order like that?
qa.a: Himani could tell didi that Rumi hides really well and ask to let Rumi play, instead of carrying out a rule that feels unkind.

qa.q: What is it like for Rumi to hear it from Himani rather than from didi?
qa.a: It probably hurts Rumi more because it came from Himani, one of the players, rather than from didi, so she sits alone on her steps with her chin on her knees 😢

grounding: Shows a child obeying the order of an older girl visiting for the holidays to exclude a playmate, uneasy but trusting that the older one knows best.

passage: The Republic Day rehearsal in the school yard at Kheda was running late, and Bhupen sir's voice was already hoarse. "Sabina, you're group leader," he said. "Tell Motilal he's out of the drill. He ruins every line. Make sure he knows it's because he doesn't practise." Sabina looked at Motilal, who was mouthing the counts to himself at the edge of the dust. Her stomach tightened. But sir had trained twenty batches; he must know. She walked over. "Sir says you're out. You don't practise." Her voice came out louder than she meant. Motilal's face crumpled, then went blank, and he sat down under the peepal tree. For the rest of rehearsal Sabina kept missing her own steps, telling herself, It was sir's order, not mine.

qa.q: What was Motilal doing at the edge of the dust?
qa.a: Motilal was mouthing the counts to himself at the edge of the dust.

qa.q: Why did Sabina go along with the order even though her stomach tightened?
qa.a: Sabina felt uneasy but reasoned that sir had trained twenty batches, so he must know better than she did.

qa.q: At which moment could Sabina have chosen differently, and how?
qa.a: When she saw Motilal quietly mouthing the counts, Sabina could have told sir that Motilal was trying and asked sir to speak to him instead.

qa.q: What might Motilal think when the message comes from Sabina?
qa.a: Motilal may feel shamed in front of the group, since he was practising and still heard 'You don't practise' from a classmate.

grounding: Illustrates a child carrying out a teacher's order to push a classmate out, uneasy but telling herself the responsibility is the teacher's.

passage: In the lunch hall of her school in Lisbon, Nadia had just been made table captain, with a yellow badge pinned to her jumper. When Gabriel knocked over his soup, the dinner supervisor, Senhora Costa, marched over. "Captain, you tell him off. Loudly, so the whole table learns." Nadia's cheeks burned. Gabriel was already dabbing at the puddle with a napkin, eyes wet. But grown-ups knew the rules, and Senhora Costa sounded very sure. "Gabriel, that's so messy!" Nadia said, loud enough for the next table to turn. Everyone stared. Afterwards Nadia pushed her rice around and told herself she had only done what she was told. Somehow that didn't make the rice taste any better.

qa.q: What was pinned to Nadia's jumper when she became table captain?
qa.a: A yellow badge was pinned to her jumper.

qa.q: How can you tell Nadia felt uneasy about scolding Gabriel?
qa.a: Nadia's cheeks burned before she spoke, and afterwards she pushed her rice around, trying to tell herself she had only done what she was told 😟

qa.q: What could Nadia have said to Senhora Costa at that moment?
qa.a: Nadia could have said quietly, "He's already cleaning it up," and helped Gabriel with the napkin instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Gabriel feel being scolded by a classmate in front of everyone?
qa.a: Gabriel, already wet-eyed and cleaning up, would likely feel embarrassed and ganged up on when the next table turned to stare.

grounding: Shows a child obeying a supervisor's order to scold a classmate publicly, uneasy but placing the responsibility on the adult.

subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]
passage: The Saturday music class at the community centre had one rule: Sir's word was final. Tanvir, ten, was row leader, which meant he stood at the end and passed out song sheets. Before the concert practice, Sir called him over. "Tell Damini to sit at the back and only listen today. She's off-key. Tell her clearly." Tanvir's hands went cold. Damini had practised the whole week; he had heard her humming at the gate. But Sir had taught music for thirty years. He must know. Tanvir walked over. "Sir says you sit at the back. You're off-key." Damini's mouth opened, then closed. She took her sheet and sat on the last bench, not singing. All through practice Tanvir kept thinking, Sir said it. Not me. His own voice sounded thin.

qa.q: What was Tanvir's job as row leader?
qa.a: He stood at the end and passed out song sheets.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel when Sir gave him the order, and how did he calm himself?
qa.a: He felt uneasy, his hands going cold, but told himself Sir had taught music for thirty years and must know best.

qa.q: What could Tanvir have done instead of passing the message on?
qa.a: He could have told Sir that Damini had practised all week and asked Sir to speak to her himself, or kindly, instead of saying it harshly for him.

qa.q: How might Damini see Tanvir after he delivered the message?
qa.a: Damini may feel hurt and embarrassed, and see Tanvir as the one who shamed her, even though the words came from Sir.

grounding: A ten-year-old obeys a teacher's order to push a classmate out of singing, feeling uneasy but reasoning that the adult must know best.

subtype: Following a grown-up's order to hurt [Actor]
passage: I'm Anjali. I study on the bench by our building's skating rink most evenings, so I saw this. Elizabeth, eight, is the coach's favourite, always first in line. On Tuesday a new girl came with old skates held together with tape. The coach skated over to Elizabeth and said something, pointing at the new girl. Elizabeth looked at the ground for a moment, then rolled over and said loudly, "Coach says you can't skate with our group. You'll slow us down." The new girl sat on the edge and unlaced her skates. Elizabeth kept looking back at her, falling more than usual. Later I heard her tell her mother, "Coach told me to. It's his rule." She said it twice, as if she needed to hear it.

qa.q: What held the new girl's old skates together?
qa.a: They were held together with tape.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth repeating 'Coach told me to' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and guilty, and was trying to push the responsibility onto the coach so she would feel better.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth's mother say when she hears this?
qa.a: She could gently ask how the new girl might have felt and help Elizabeth think of a way to include her next time, even if the coach said otherwise.

qa.q: What was the session like for the new girl?
qa.a: She was told by another child, in front of the group, that she could not join, and she spent the time on the edge unlacing her skates alone.

grounding: A child obeys a coach's instruction to exclude a new girl, and later insists it was the coach's rule, as seen by an onlooker.
